title: Spanish Protesters Rally at Parliament as Emergency Housing Decrees Face Rejection】
body:
MADRID — Spain’s left‑leaning government suffered a decisive setback on Friday when parliament rejected a suite of emergency decrees intended to curb a rapidly worsening housing crisis. The vote, which saw the Catalan nationalist bloc Junts‑per‑Catalunya break ranks with the centre‑right Popular Party (PP) and the far‑right Vox, left Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s administration without the legislative tools it had hoped would rein in soaring rents and protect vulnerable tenants.

The rejected package comprised three measures: a temporary freeze on rent increases in “high‑demand” cities, a boost to public housing construction, and stricter penalties for landlords who evict tenants without just cause. Proponents argued the decrees were a necessary, time‑limited response to a market that has seen rents climb by more than 30 % in the past two years, especially in Madrid, Barcelona, and other urban hubs. Critics, however, labeled the proposals as “populist overreach” that would deter investment, shrink the rental supply, and undermine property rights.

The parliamentary showdown unfolded amid a broader political stalemate. Sánchez’s Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) holds a fragile minority government that relies on the support of smaller leftist parties, such as Unidas Podemos, to pass legislation. While the coalition partners backed the housing emergency plan, Junts‑per‑Catalunya – a regional party that has been negotiating a separate agenda on Catalan autonomy – voted against it, citing concerns that the decrees would set a precedent for central interference in regional markets. The PP, led by opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, and Vox, under Santiago Abascal, seized on the vote to portray the government as economically reckless, promising instead market‑driven solutions that they claim will increase housing supply through deregulation and tax incentives for developers.

Housing affordability has become one of the most potent political flashpoints in Spain, a country that emerged from a decade‑long recession only to confront a new crisis spurred by low interest rates, foreign investment, and a surge in short‑term rentals. According to the National Statistics Institute, the median rent for a two‑bedroom apartment in Madrid now exceeds €1,200 per month, a level that many young professionals and low‑income families cannot sustain. The crisis has also fueled a wave of street protests, with thousands gathering outside the Congreso de los Diputados on Friday, chanting slogans such as “¡Vivienda digna ya!” (“Decent housing now!”) and demanding swift action from the government.

Analysts warn that the parliamentary defeat could have far‑reaching consequences for Sánchez’s agenda. Without the emergency housing measures, the administration may struggle to quell public discontent ahead of the upcoming municipal elections in 2027, where housing policy is expected to be a decisive issue. Moreover, the loss underscores the challenges of governing with a fragmented parliament, where regional parties can swing outcomes on key votes. Some political scientists suggest that Sánchez might seek to renegotiate the decrees, trimming the most contentious provisions to win over Junts‑per‑Catalunya and other holdouts, or alternatively, push for a broader legislative package that pairs rent controls with incentives for new construction to appease both social and market‑oriented critics.

Looking ahead, the government is expected to regroup and explore alternative avenues to address the housing squeeze. Possible strategies include accelerating the rollout of Spain’s “Plan Estatal de Vivienda,” expanding subsidies for first‑time homebuyers, and encouraging municipalities to adopt local rent‑control ordinances. International observers note that Spain’s experience mirrors a wider European trend, where governments are grappling with balancing tenant protections against the need to maintain a vibrant rental market. As the debate continues, the pressure on policymakers to deliver concrete solutions will only intensify, with the next parliamentary session likely to become a pivotal battleground for Spain’s housing future.
